title: Synchronous OPFS open-by-path for dedicated workers
body:
Hello, I'm the lead developer of [Reflex++](https://reflexplusplus.dev/), a cross-platform C++ framework for building applications that run natively and in the browser ([live demo](https://www.newsonicarts.com/apps/granite)). I'm following up on #100, closed in February 2024.

Our use case requires a synchronous way for a dedicated worker to open an OPFS file by path and obtain a FileSystemSyncAccessHandle.

In our browser implementation, the C++ application's main thread runs in a dedicated worker, with additional C++ threads running in their own workers. Our portable filesystem API follows the conventional synchronous C++ contract: opening a file must return a usable handle before execution continues.

We understand the web platform's preference for asynchronous operations on the browser's main thread. However, dedicated workers already support blocking operations, and OPFS explicitly provides synchronous reads and writes for this reason.

The difficulty is that createSyncAccessHandle() itself remains asynchronous.

This currently forces us to use a separate I/O worker to open files. Since FileSystemSyncAccessHandle cannot be transferred between workers, that worker must also perform subsequent reads and writes. Every synchronous C++ file operation therefore requires cross-worker messaging and synchronization, even though the calling thread is already a dedicated worker capable of performing synchronous I/O.

As discussed in #100, making createSyncAccessHandle() synchronous alone would not solve the general problem, since getDirectoryHandle() and getFileHandle() are also asynchronous. What we really need is a fully synchronous path from OPFS directory lookup through to opening a usable access handle, restricted to dedicated workers.

We appreciate that JSPI offers another approach to integrating asynchronous APIs with WebAssembly. However, JSPI makes asynchronous operations appear synchronous to calling code by suspending and resuming execution; it does not provide a genuinely blocking filesystem API. Introducing that suspension model into an existing multithreaded C++ runtime is not a trivial substitute for synchronous filesystem operations.

A synchronous OPFS opening path would allow each application thread to open and access files directly, eliminating the I/O worker, cross-worker dispatch overhead, and much of the synchronization complexity. More importantly, it would preserve the same filesystem contract across our supported platforms without requiring application-level changes.

I hope this use case might influence your thinking on synchronous OPFS file opening in dedicated workers.  Is there a particular technical or architectural reason why synchronous file opening and directory traversal cannot be supported in dedicated workers? From our perspective, given that potentially time consuming synchronous reads and writes are permitted, it's not immediately clear why synchronous opening and directory traversal are treated differently. We'd be interested to understand the constraints behind this distinction.

More broadly, we believe that enabling the next generation of high-performance, desktop-class applications on the web means giving developers the right tools at the right level of abstraction. Promises and asynchronous APIs are invaluable for much of the web, but worker-based runtimes also benefit from direct, low-level synchronous operations where blocking is explicitly allowed. Supporting both approaches would make the web a more capable platform for sophisticated native-style applications, without compromising responsiveness and the user experience on the main thread.
